title: Camp Paw & Passage
clue: One night away, a bit of canvas, and a spot that will be named for wherever your dog decides.
reveal: A real overnight at a dog-welcoming campground. Before a single peg goes in, your dog finds where they settle, and the whole camp is built around that spot and named after it.
objective: Spend one night at a dog-welcoming campground, build camp around the spot your dog chooses, and make a camp patch to mark it.
instructions: Book a dog-welcoming pitch for one night. Confirm the pet policy, fees, leash limit, quiet hours and whether dogs may sleep in the tent. Choose a mild forecast and a drive-up pitch for a first trip. If you have done The Tent Rehearsal, bring its trip bag.

Pack your dog's bed and blanket from home, usual food and plenty of water, a six-foot leash, ID tag, vaccination papers, towels and a light for dusk. Use a car harness or crate, take breaks, and never leave your dog in the car.
Arrive in daylight. Before unpacking, walk the pitch together on leash and let your dog sniff round. Watch where they first settle or linger. That spot is Camp Centre.

Build camp around Camp Centre: bed beside it, bowl in reach, your chairs and tent close by. Keep the layout like home. Name the camp after what is there, such as Camp Sunny Rock, and write the name on a card or fabric scrap for your patch.
Feed your dog their usual meal at camp, then stow all food and rubbish away from wildlife. Take a slow evening loop on leash, with a light on you both.
Settle in with a lantern and the leash on, away from the fire pit. Keep your dog with you; never tie them out or leave them alone in the tent. Let them choose where to sleep.
In the morning, take a sunrise stroll, check your dog's paws, coat and ears for ticks and burrs, then pack up while they rest on their bed.
Pin or stitch your camp patch to a bag or hang it on the lead hook as the proof of your first camp.
twist: Your dog picks the heart of camp: wherever they first settle becomes Camp Centre, and the bed, the chairs and even the camp's name are arranged around it.
variations: Easier: choose a campsite with a cabin or camper hire, a hard-standing pitch and a short walk to facilities.
Day camp: book a pitch or picnic area for the afternoon, build camp around Camp Centre, and skip the night.
Seated version: pick a drive-up pitch with level ground, set up a chair at Camp Centre, and let your dog roam the leash length.
Compact version: a single night with the car parked close, heading home early if the weather turns or your dog is unsettled.
completion: You have spent a night at camp with your dog beside you, built around the spot they chose, and made a patch to mark it.
photoIdea: Your dog resting at Camp Centre with the tent or lantern glowing behind, taken from a respectful distance.
memoryPrompt: Where did your dog first settle, and what did you call the camp?
supplies: Your dog's own bed and blanket
Six-foot leash, harness and ID tag
Card or fabric scrap and a pen
substitutes: A flashlight with a cloth over it instead of a lantern
A cardboard circle instead of a fabric patch

reservation.note: Book a dog-welcoming pitch ahead and confirm pet rules, fees, tent or cabin rules, quiet hours and leash length with the campsite.

dietNotes: Feed only your dog's usual food and portions, nothing new on the trip, and ask your vet about travel diet. Treats are optional; a calm evening works without any food extras.
safety: Keep your dog with you day and night; never leave them alone in a tent, tied up, or in a car.
Leash at camp, ID on, food and rubbish stored away; watch for wildlife, ticks and fire pits.
Check night temperatures and the ground; insulate the bed, and head home if your dog shivers, pants or is unsettled.
